country.comment: Two glacierized watersheds in the Peruvian Andes are studied: the Santa River watershed (Ancash and coastal plain, Peru) and the Shullcas River watershed draining to Huancayo (Junin, Peru).

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive survey statistics are reported for household water access continuity and perceived dry-season shortages, while the analysis of legal, property, and governance mechanisms (water-rights formalization, customary usufruct vs. formal licensing, stalled basin council) is qualitative with no numeric regression/causal effect estimate linking institutional variables to water outcomes.
effect_estimate.value: In urban Huancayo (Shullcas basin, n = 911 households, Dec 2015), <50% of households had constant (20-24 hours/day) water access and ~20% had <10 hours/day despite 100% dry-season river diversion and 18 municipal wells. In three Santa River highland catchments (n = 125 households, 2008-2009), perceived dry-season water supply decline was 93% ± 3.6% in Querococha (3% glacierized), 81% ± 6.54% in Quilcay (17% glacierized), and 76% ± 11% in Llanganuco (36% glacierized), with <10% reporting domestic water shortages and ~25% reporting irrigation shortages. Regarding legal and institutional mechanisms (Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported): rural water access depends on spatial proximity of property claims/grazing allotments to springs and streams; Santa watershed council formation initiated in 2010 stalled due to regional/inter-regional politics, leaving dry-season scarcity managed ad hoc; and universal volumetric water-rights formalization under Peru's 2009 Hydrologic Resources Law (via PROFODUA) saw upper-basin irrigators refuse registration in defense of customary usufruct rights or find volumetric licenses abstract without gauging infrastructure while community institutions retain local control, whereas large coastal users secure formal rights and transfer up to 90% of dry-season Santa discharge above intakes, generating disputes over overlapping legal and customary water rights.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 22-29, Sections 4.3.1-4.3.3; PDF pp. 35-36, Section 5; PDF p. 42, Table 1; PDF p. 50, Figure 7

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods case study (MMAT ceiling = 2) that directly documents legal, property, and governance mechanisms (PROFODUA volumetric water-rights formalization and irrigator refusal to register, overlapping customary usufruct and state licensing regimes, stalled multi-sectoral watershed council formation, and property-claim proximity to springs) through primary key-informant interviews, participant observation, household surveys, and legal/administrative records.

sample_size.comment: Multi-component empirical study reporting sample sizes across two household surveys, qualitative interviews in two watersheds, hydrochemical water sampling, and remote-sensing land-cover scenes; exact N of key-informant interviews in the Santa watershed is not reported.
sample_size.value: 125 households (543 people) across 3 Santa River tributary watersheds (40 Querococha, 32 Quilcay, 53 Llanganuco; 2008-2009 survey); 911 households in Huancayo (December 2015 urban water access survey); 10 semi-structured and unstructured interviews in the Shullcas watershed (2014-2015); unspecified number of key-informant interviews in the Santa watershed; 177 water samples (90 in 4 Cordillera Blanca watersheds, 2008-2009; 87 in Shullcas basin, 2014); 2 Landsat TM images (1990 and 2011) covering 2,323 km2
